summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ , a man with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis and neurogenic bladder managed with a chronic Foley catheter, was admitted for evaluation of gross hematuria following a recent traumatic catheter change. He had no fever, pain, or signs of systemic infection. Labs showed bacteriuria and pyuria, but clinical assessment concluded this represented asymptomatic colonization rather than active urinary tract infection. The hematuria was attributed to urethral trauma during catheter replacement and resolved without intervention. His chronic unintentional weight loss was evaluated with normal thyroid, inflammatory, metabolic, and imaging studies; outpatient cancer screening was recommended. He remained neurologically stable, continued on home medications including fluoxetine and oxybutynin, and was discharged home after 3 days with instructions to monitor for symptoms and follow up with primary care and specialists.
